description:
🦅 ¡Únete a KUNTUR X! 

¡Hola! Soy estudiante de Medicina Humana de la Universidad Norbert Wiener, actualmente en el internado médico. Me apasionan la investigación científica, la neurociencia, la neurocirugía, la ingeniería biomédica y la medicina aeroespacial.

En KUNTUR X queremos desarrollar una propuesta innovadora para el monitoreo de la salud de los astronautas, integrando medicina, neurociencia, ingeniería e inteligencia artificial.

KUNTUR X: From the Andes to the Stars.
summary:
KAWSAY (Quechua for "life") is an on-board, explainable health-triage system for astronauts, built first for Artemis IV (2028). Two crew members will spend about a week near the lunar South Pole, where NASA notes that direct contact with Earth is limited, and the crew medical officer is often not a physician. In 2020, a jugular vein clot on the ISS was managed with doctors on Earth in real time; KAWSAY is designed for when that is not possible.
Every day the crew log vital signs, sleep and any new symptoms. When symptoms appear, a transparent rule engine scores them with NEWS2, the UK's standard early warning score, applies 32 guideline-based triage rules (16 built from NASA evidence) and compares the values with the astronaut's own baseline. In seconds it returns one of five levels with clear actions: what to do now, how often to recheck, when to contact Earth and when to escalate. AI never makes the decision.
In a pilot with 10 randomly chosen cases, KAWSAY assigned the correct level in 9; published symptom checkers were correct in 57%.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

KAWSAY gives astronauts and their crew medical officer a fast, explainable answer to one question: does this health problem need action, and how urgently? In 2020, a jugular vein clot found on the ISS was managed with physicians on Earth guiding the crew in real time (NEJM 2020). KAWSAY is designed for when that live support is not available. Our first target is Artemis IV (2028): two astronauts will spend about a week near the lunar South Pole, where NASA notes that direct communication with Earth is limited without relays, and the crew medical officer is often a non-physician with about 40 hours of medical training.

HOW IT WORKS

The system follows four phases. (1) Triage on admission: identification, medical history, usual medication, drug reactions and baseline vital signs. (2) Daily check every 24 hours: a full report with vital signs measured with validated devices and a step-by-step measurement guide, sleep and sleepiness (Karolinska Sleepiness Scale) and a check for new symptoms; between reports, a smartwatch tracks trends continuously. (3) Alert phase when symptoms appear: a 17-item symptom checklist, NEWS2 (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen, systolic blood pressure, heart rate, level of consciousness and temperature) and, for milder cases, time since onset, course and pain assessment. (4) Report: a second, healthy crew member sends the result to the physician on Earth at the next link. A rule engine, not AI, applies 32 triage rules taken from clinical guidelines (for example AHA/ACC chest pain, BTS oxygen, ESC syncope, Surviving Sepsis) and compares the values with the astronaut's own baseline. The most urgent rule always wins, and missing data is flagged instead of guessed. A physician dashboard shows each crew member's status, trends and data provenance. A local language model (Ollama) is being integrated only to explain results in plain words; it never decides the level.

WHAT THE CREW SEES

Each level comes with concrete actions. EMERGENCY: check response and breathing, give oxygen if saturation is below 94%, note the time of onset, stay with the crew member and recheck continuously. PRIORITY: repeat the abnormal reading and have the medical officer review within 1 hour, rechecking every hour. SCHEDULED: review within 24 hours and recheck every 4 to 6 hours. SELF-CARE: use the kit item for that alert and recheck at least every 12 hours. INSUFFICIENT DATA: measure again with the correct technique; no level is assigned without complete data. Recheck intervals follow the NEWS2 clinical response chart and NICE; first-response steps follow the American Heart Association and the British Thoracic Society. Every level also states when to escalate.

NASA DATA AND SCIENTIFIC BASIS

NASA documents and NASA-led studies with astronaut data were used to write 16 of the 32 rules, to build 11 of the 15 spaceflight test cases and to define the mission context. Examples: the NASA urinary health technical brief (kidney stones, urinary retention, infection), symptoms in 46 long-duration ISS crew members (Crucian 2016, NASA Johnson Space Center), jugular venous stasis in 6 of 11 astronauts (Marshall-Goebel 2019), SANS (Lee 2020) and astronaut sleep (Barger 2014). NASA's Earth Independent Medical Operations concept describes the need for this kind of on-board support. NEWS2, the backbone score, predicted death within 24 hours with an AUROC of 0.89 in more than 250,000 hospital admissions (Pimentel 2019). Every rule cites its sources; the full list has 77 references. The demo runs on synthetic data and contains no individual astronaut records.

BENEFITS

All of a crew member's health data in one place; a triage level and clear next steps in seconds, on board; reasons that a non-physician can follow and a flight surgeon can audit later; and a daily record that turns small changes from each astronaut's own baseline into early warnings.

POTENTIAL

Artemis IV is the first step. The same engine fits longer surface stays, Gateway and Mars missions, where each message can take up to 22 minutes one way and NASA's Integrated Medical Model expects about 166 medical events in a 16-month transit with four crew. Because it is designed to run locally on a tablet or laptop, without specialist hardware, the same approach can serve places on Earth that share the problem: Antarctic stations, ships at sea, and remote Andean and Amazonian communities in Peru, where a physician may be days away. Its rules are open and editable, so space agencies and health services can review them, adapt them and add rules for their own setting.

PILOT RESULT AND FULL EVALUATION

In a pilot, 10 cases were chosen at random with RANDOM.ORG (7 of the 31 adult cases of the BMJ benchmark and 3 of the 15 spaceflight cases) and entered in the application as simulated patients. KAWSAY assigned the correct level in 9 of 10 (90%) [MISSED CASE]. In the original BMJ study, online symptom checkers gave correct triage advice in 57% of cases. The pilot is small and is not a validation. The full evaluation follows a protocol based on STARD 2015: 31 adult benchmark cases and 15 spaceflight cases, with the two physicians on the team assigning reference levels blind to the application, a frozen software version and a single official run. The randomization screenshots are in our repository.

TOOLS

Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, React, HTML/CSS and SQL; PGlite for the local in-browser demo, with components ready for PostgreSQL and Docker; Ollama for the local explanation model (in development); a telemetry simulator with synthetic data. Planning and protocol figures were made in Miro.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a black-box AI, KAWSAY combines a hospital-proven early warning score, guideline red flags and each astronaut's personal baseline in one transparent flow designed for a crew of two with limited medical support. Every decision is linked to the rule and the published source that triggered it, and the two physicians on our team review each rule.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Measurement quality (validated devices, a full 60-second respiratory count, oximeter limits with cold skin, darker skin and low perfusion), missing data, differences between crew members, ease of use under stress, limited communication and failure of the language model. We also state our limits: the demo uses synthetic data only, has no continuous physical sensors yet and has no clinical or spaceflight validation, and NEWS2 was validated in hospital patients on Earth, not in reduced gravity. However, the foundations are strong. NEWS2 is the national standard for detecting acute deterioration in UK hospitals, is recommended by NICE, and predicted death within 24 hours with an AUROC of 0.89 in more than 250,000 admissions (Pimentel 2019). Every one of the 32 rules comes from an international guideline or from NASA and astronaut studies, and comparing each value with the astronaut's own baseline helps to account for the changes in heart rate and blood pressure that occur in reduced gravity. Because the rules are transparent, physicians and flight surgeons can audit and correct each one, and the pilot already gave the correct level in 9 of 10 randomly chosen cases.
